reason: Sources S1 and S3 provide 18 matching claims regarding vacuum exposure effects, including specific NASA accident accounts and physiological details.
story: Movies show people exploding in space, but you won’t burst. Your skin is tough enough to contain the pressure, and your blood won’t boil. You also won’t freeze instantly because heat loss is slow in a vacuum. Instead, you’ll experience ebullism: gas bubbles forming in your fluids that can bloat you to twice your size. The real danger is hypoxia. Your lungs actually strip oxygen from your blood, leaving you with just 15 seconds of consciousness. NASA technician Jim LeBlanc survived a 1960s vacuum chamber accident. His last memory before passing out was the saliva on his tongue beginning to bubble. He was rescued and recovered, proving you have roughly 90 seconds to be saved before it’s fatal.
angle: In a vacuum, your body won't explode, but you will bloat to twice your size while your saliva bubbles on your tongue.

claims.claim: A human body exposed to the vacuum of space does not explode or burst.
The strength of human skin is sufficient to prevent the body from bursting in a vacuum.
Internal circulatory pressure prevents blood from boiling during vacuum exposure.
Ebullism occurs in a vacuum, causing gas bubbles to form in body fluids.
The human body can bloat or swell up to twice its normal size due to ebullism.
Sudden freezing does not happen in a vacuum because heat transfer is slow.
Heat loss in space occurs only through radiation.
Useful consciousness is lost in approximately 10 to 15 seconds.
In a vacuum, the lungs reverse their function and strip oxygen from the blood.
Hypoxia, or lack of oxygen reaching the brain, is the cause of unconsciousness.
A human has roughly 90 seconds to two minutes to be recompressed before death occurs.
Holding your breath during sudden decompression causes damage to the lungs.
Exposure to vacuum for under 30 seconds is unlikely to cause permanent physical damage.
NASA test subject Jim LeBlanc survived an accidental vacuum chamber decompression in the mid-1960s.
LeBlanc remained conscious for about 14 to 15 seconds after his suit leaked.
LeBlanc's last memory before passing out was the saliva on his tongue bubbling or boiling.
Pilot Joe Kittinger's hand was exposed to near-vacuum during a record high-altitude jump in 1960.
Kittinger's exposed hand became painful and useless but returned to normal at lower altitudes.

disputed: The exact date of Jim LeBlanc's accident is cited as 1965 in S3 and 1966 in S1; the script should use 'mid-1960s'.
The exact pressure LeBlanc's suit reached is cited as 0.1 psi in S1 and less than 1 psi in S3; attribute as 'less than 1 psi'.
The duration LeBlanc remained conscious is cited as 14 seconds in S1 and 15 seconds in S3; attribute as 'about 15 seconds'.
